_comment: Authored, topic-tagged curriculum questions used by module checkpoints. Unlike the upload-to-quiz flow these are not model generated, so topic mastery is measured against stable, reviewed items.

T01.stem: A household survey draws its sample from a list of dwellings compiled three years ago. Newly constructed colonies are absent from that list. What error does this introduce?
options: Processing error at the tabulation stage
Sampling error that shrinks as n grows
Non-response bias among listed households
Under-coverage of the target population
T01.explanation: Units that exist in the population but are missing from the frame are under-covered. This is a frame defect, not a sampling or processing problem.

T01.stem: Why can post-survey weighting NOT repair coverage error in the sampling frame?
options: Weighting is only valid for stratified designs
Coverage error affects only the variance, never the point estimate
Weights must sum to the sample size, not the population
Units missing from the frame had no chance of selection, so no respondent represents them
T01.explanation: Weighting redistributes the responses you did obtain. A unit with zero selection probability is represented by nobody, so no weight can stand in for it.

T01.stem: A frame lists some commercial premises twice under slightly different names. If this is not detected, the estimates will be affected by:
options: Under-coverage of the commercial sector
Over-coverage, giving those units an inflated chance of selection
A reduction in the design effect
Imputation bias
T01.explanation: Duplicate frame entries are over-coverage: the duplicated unit has roughly twice the selection probability it should have.

T01.stem: For rural household surveys in India, the sampling frame at the first stage is most commonly built from:
options: A list of registered enterprises
Village lists from the Census
Ration card registers
The electoral roll of the district
T01.explanation: Census village lists provide the standard first-stage frame in rural areas; urban areas use Census enumeration blocks.

T02.stem: Stratification reduces the variance of an estimator most when strata are:
options: Formed at random from the frame
Internally varied so each contains the full range of values
Equal in size regardless of their composition
Internally homogeneous and different from each other on the study variable
T02.explanation: The gain comes from removing between-stratum variation from the sampling error. Homogeneous strata that differ from one another maximise that gain.

T02.stem: Under proportional allocation, the number of units sampled from a stratum is set in proportion to:
options: The size of the stratum in the population
The cost of enumerating one unit in the stratum
The response rate achieved in the previous round
The variance of the study variable in the stratum
T02.explanation: Proportional allocation uses stratum size alone. Optimal (Neyman) allocation is what brings variance and cost into the calculation.

T02.stem: Optimal allocation assigns a LARGER sample to a stratum when that stratum has:
options: The highest previous response rate
Low variability and high cost per unit
High variability in the study variable and low cost per unit
The smallest population size
T02.explanation: Neyman allocation puts effort where variance is high and enumeration is cheap; both push the allocated sample up.

T02.stem: An officer stratifies an establishment survey by employment size band. This is sensible mainly because:
options: Turnover and employment are strongly related, so size bands are homogeneous on the study variable
Size bands always contain equal numbers of establishments
It guarantees a higher response rate
It removes the need for weighting
T02.explanation: A good stratifier correlates with the study variable. Establishment size does, which is why size-band stratification is near-universal.

T03.stem: The design weight of a sampled unit is:
options: Its probability of selection
The number of units in its stratum
The ratio of the sample size to the population size
The reciprocal of its probability of selection
T03.explanation: A unit selected with probability 1/500 represents about 500 units, so its design weight is 500.

T03.stem: In a two-stage design, villages are selected with probability proportional to population and a fixed number of households is taken in each. The effect on household selection probabilities is that they are:
options: Highest in the smallest villages
Proportional to village population
Undefined without a listing of all households
Approximately equal across villages, making the design self-weighting
T03.explanation: PPS at stage one and a fixed take at stage two offset each other, producing roughly equal overall probabilities. This is the classic self-weighting design.

T03.stem: Calibration adjusts survey weights so that:
options: Weighted survey totals match known population benchmarks
Imputed values equal the observed mean
Every respondent carries the same weight
The sample size matches the target
T03.explanation: Calibration forces agreement with external totals such as projected population by age and sex, reducing bias and often variance.

T03.stem: Treating a multi-stage stratified sample as if it were a simple random sample when estimating variance will typically:
options: Bias the point estimate upward
Understate the standard errors
Overstate the standard errors
Leave standard errors unchanged
T03.explanation: Clustering makes observations within a PSU positively correlated. Ignoring it understates variance, sometimes badly.

T04.stem: An edit rule flags a record where a respondent's age is 12 and marital status is 'widowed'. This is best described as:
options: An imputation rule
A range edit on a single field
A consistency edit between two related fields
An outlier detection rule
T04.explanation: Range edits check one field against permitted values; consistency edits check the relationship between fields, as here.

T04.stem: The purpose of selective editing is to:
options: Edit every record to the same standard
Remove all records that fail any edit rule
Concentrate limited review effort on records whose correction would most change the published aggregate
Replace failed records with imputed values automatically
T04.explanation: Selective editing scores records by their likely influence on the estimate, so scarce analyst time goes where it changes the published figure.

T04.stem: A large establishment reports turnover 40 times its previous return. Before treating this as an outlier, the analyst should FIRST:
options: Check whether a genuine change such as a merger or unit-of-measure error explains it
Delete the record from the dataset
Replace the value with the industry mean
Reduce the weight of the record to zero
T04.explanation: Extreme values are often real or a simple unit error (rupees versus lakh). Investigate before altering, since large units carry heavy weight.

T04.stem: Over-editing is a risk because it:
options: Always increases the response rate
Consumes resources and can introduce bias by smoothing genuine variation
Removes the need for imputation
Reduces the sample size below the design target
T04.explanation: Editing everything costs time and can quietly pull true extreme values toward the middle, biasing dispersion measures.

T05.stem: Data are 'missing completely at random' (MCAR) when the probability of a value being missing:
options: Is the same in every stratum by design
Depends only on observed variables
Depends on the missing value itself
Does not depend on observed or unobserved data
T05.explanation: MCAR is the strongest and rarest assumption. MAR depends on observed data; MNAR depends on the unobserved value itself.

T05.stem: Compared with mean imputation, hot-deck donor imputation is generally preferred because it:
options: Removes the need to record which values were imputed
Guarantees an unbiased point estimate
Preserves the distribution of the variable rather than piling values at the mean
Is faster to compute
T05.explanation: Mean imputation artificially shrinks variance. Donor methods take a real value from a similar responding unit, keeping the shape of the distribution.

T05.stem: Why must imputed values be flagged in the microdata?
options: Flagging is required before weighting can be applied
Imputation adds uncertainty that naive variance estimates ignore
It allows imputed records to be deleted before publication
Imputed values are always wrong
T05.explanation: Treating imputed values as if they were observed understates variance. The flag lets users apply methods that account for imputation uncertainty.

T05.stem: Item non-response differs from unit non-response in that item non-response is:
options: A missing answer to some questions from a responding unit
A record deleted during editing
A unit missing from the sampling frame
A refusal by the entire household to participate
T05.explanation: Unit non-response means the whole unit is lost and is handled by weighting; item non-response is handled by imputation.

options: Can be estimated directly from the sample variance
Does not necessarily shrink as the sample size grows
Only occurs in censuses
Is removed by increasing the number of strata
T06.explanation: Doubling the sample can double the volume of measurement and processing error. Only sampling error is guaranteed to fall with n.

T06.stem: In large official surveys, non-sampling error compared with sampling error is:
options: Equal by construction
Always negligible
Always smaller because of training
Frequently larger in magnitude
T06.explanation: At large sample sizes sampling error is small, which leaves measurement, processing and non-response as the dominant error sources.

T06.stem: Independent re-interview of a subsample is used primarily to:
options: Replace non-responding households
Calibrate the design weights
Increase the effective sample size
Measure response and interviewer error
T06.explanation: Re-interview compares an independent measurement against the original to quantify measurement and interviewer variance.

T06.stem: A quality report accompanying a statistical release would normally include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: The imputation rate
The identities of individual respondents
The response rate
Coefficients of variation for key estimates
T06.explanation: Respondent identity is protected by statistical confidentiality. Response, imputation and precision measures are standard quality indicators.

T07.stem: Which question is double-barrelled and should be split?
options: How many persons usually reside in this household?
In the last 30 days, did you seek medical treatment?
Are you satisfied with the quality and the timeliness of the release?
What is your principal occupation?
T07.explanation: It asks about two attributes at once. A respondent satisfied with quality but not timeliness cannot answer accurately.

T07.stem: A closed question with pre-coded options is preferred over an open question mainly when:
options: The full range of plausible answers is known in advance
The interviewer is inexperienced
The subject is sensitive
The sample size is small
T07.explanation: Pre-coding is only safe when the option list is exhaustive. If it is not, open capture with later coding avoids forcing wrong answers.

T07.stem: Lengthening the recall period in a consumption survey from 7 days to 30 days typically:
options: Has no effect on reported expenditure
Improves accuracy for all item types equally
Reduces recall accuracy for small frequent purchases
Eliminates telescoping error
T07.explanation: Longer reference periods lose small, frequent items to forgetting; short periods suit frequent purchases and long periods suit rare large ones.

T07.stem: A response scale offering 'Excellent, Good, Good, Poor' is defective because the options are not:
options: Balanced in length
Written in the local language
Ordered alphabetically
Mutually exclusive
T07.explanation: Duplicated categories mean the same answer maps to two codes, so responses cannot be interpreted.

T08.stem: Sensitive questions are usually placed late in an interview because:
options: Early questions must be closed-ended
They take longer to answer
The respondent has invested time and rapport has been built
Interviewers memorise them last
T08.explanation: Asking sensitive items early risks a break-off that costs the whole interview. Late placement means earlier answers are already secured.

T08.stem: A skip pattern instructs the interviewer to:
options: Return to a previous section for verification
Omit every third question to save time
Record a non-response code
Bypass questions that do not apply given an earlier answer
T08.explanation: Filters route the respondent past inapplicable blocks, for instance skipping employment detail for a respondent not in the labour force.

T08.stem: Opening a household questionnaire with straightforward demographic items rather than income questions is intended to:
options: Establish rapport and reduce early break-off
Satisfy a legal requirement
Improve the sampling frame
Reduce the total interview length
T08.explanation: Easy, non-threatening openers build cooperation before harder material arrives.

T08.stem: In a paper instrument, a complex nest of skip instructions is risky chiefly because:
options: It increases printing cost
It prevents stratification
Interviewers may misroute, creating missing or invalid data
It requires longer reference periods
T08.explanation: Manual routing errors are a well documented source of item non-response on paper; CAPI enforces routing automatically.

T09.stem: The main data-quality advantage of CAPI over a paper schedule is that CAPI:
options: Removes the need for a sampling frame
Enforces skip patterns and range checks at the moment of collection
Guarantees a higher response rate
Eliminates the need for supervision
T09.explanation: Validating at the doorstep prevents errors that would otherwise be found weeks later in editing, when the respondent is unreachable.

T09.stem: A CAPI hard check should be reserved for values that are:
options: Merely unusual but possible
Logically impossible, since it blocks the interviewer from proceeding
Sensitive in nature
Slow to type
T09.explanation: Hard checks on merely unusual values force interviewers to enter false data to move on. Soft warnings suit implausible-but-possible values.

T09.stem: CATI is generally less suitable than CAPI for rural household surveys in India mainly because of:
options: The absence of skip logic in CATI systems
The cost of software licences
Uneven telephone coverage, which biases who can be reached
Longer questionnaire length
T09.explanation: Telephone frames under-cover exactly the households of most interest, introducing coverage bias that weighting cannot fully repair.

T09.stem: Paradata such as interview timestamps and question timings are useful mainly for:
options: Calibrating weights
Detecting interviewer falsification and problem questions
Building the sampling frame
Estimating population totals
T09.explanation: Implausibly fast interviews or a question that consistently takes very long are signals for supervision and instrument revision.

T10.stem: Household income in a district is strongly right-skewed by a few very high earners. The better measure of a typical household is the:
options: Standard deviation
Arithmetic mean
Median
Range
T10.explanation: The mean is pulled toward the long right tail. The median is unaffected by how extreme the extremes are.

T10.stem: The coefficient of variation is useful because it:
options: Expresses dispersion relative to the mean, allowing comparison across different units
Removes the effect of outliers
Is always smaller than the standard deviation
Converts any distribution to a normal one
T10.explanation: As a ratio it is unitless, so the variability of turnover in rupees can be compared with the variability of employment in persons.

T10.stem: In a cross-tabulation of employment status by education level, the cell percentages should be computed on the row total when the question of interest is:
options: How employment status differs across education levels
The overall share of graduates
How many people are in each cell
The sampling error of the table
T10.explanation: Percentaging within the explanatory category (education) lets you compare the outcome distribution across those categories.

T10.stem: A distribution with a long left tail is described as:
options: Bimodal
Leptokurtic
Positively skewed
Negatively skewed
T10.explanation: Skew is named for the direction of the tail; a long left tail means negative skew, with mean typically below median.

T11.stem: The standard error of a sample mean measures:
options: The largest error made by any interviewer
The bias introduced by non-response
The spread of individual values in the population
How much the sample mean would vary across repeated samples
T11.explanation: The standard deviation describes individuals; the standard error describes the sampling distribution of the estimate itself.

T11.stem: To halve the standard error of a mean under simple random sampling, the sample size must be multiplied by approximately:
T11.explanation: The standard error falls with the square root of n, so a fourfold increase in sample size halves it. Precision is expensive.

T11.stem: A 95% confidence interval for mean household size is 4.1 to 4.5. The correct interpretation is that:
options: Under repeated sampling, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean
There is a 95% probability the true mean lies in this particular interval
The sample mean has a 5% chance of being wrong
95% of households have between 4.1 and 4.5 members
T11.explanation: The confidence level is a property of the procedure across repetitions, not a probability statement about one fixed interval.

T11.stem: The design effect of a survey compares its variance with that of:
options: A census of the population
A simple random sample of the same size
The previous round of the same survey
A stratified sample of twice the size
T11.explanation: Deff above 1 means clustering has cost precision relative to SRS; it is the standard summary of a complex design's efficiency.

options: The result will replicate 97% of the time
The effect size is 3%
There is a 3% probability the null hypothesis is true
If the null hypothesis were true, data this extreme would occur 3% of the time
T12.explanation: The p-value is computed assuming the null is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and says nothing about replication.

T12.stem: A Type I error occurs when an analyst:
options: Uses the wrong test statistic
Selects an unrepresentative sample
Rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true
Fails to reject a null hypothesis that is false
T12.explanation: Type I is a false positive, controlled by the significance level. Type II is a false negative, controlled by power and sample size.

T12.stem: With a very large sample, a statistically significant difference may still be unimportant because:
options: p-values cannot be computed for large samples
Large samples always violate the assumptions of the test
The null hypothesis becomes untestable
Significance testing detects tiny effects that carry no practical meaning
T12.explanation: Significance answers 'is there an effect', not 'is it big enough to matter'. Always report the effect size alongside the p-value.

T12.stem: Increasing the sample size in a hypothesis test primarily increases:
options: The effect size
The power to detect a real effect
The significance level
The probability of a Type I error
T12.explanation: Power is the chance of rejecting a false null. The significance level is chosen by the analyst, not driven by n.

T13.stem: In R, a column of district names read from a CSV is stored as a factor. Applying as.numeric() directly to it returns:
options: An error that halts the script
NA for every element
The integer codes of the factor levels, not the original values
The original text unchanged
T13.explanation: Factors are integers with labels. The safe idiom is as.numeric(as.character(x)); the direct conversion silently returns level codes.

T13.stem: A data frame differs from a matrix in R in that a data frame:
options: Must be square
Stores only numeric values
Cannot be indexed by column name
Can hold different types in different columns
T13.explanation: A matrix is a single type throughout; a data frame is a list of equal-length vectors that may each have their own type.

T13.stem: A survey file codes 'not applicable' as 99. If read without instruction, R will:
options: Refuse to read the column
Automatically convert it to NA
Store the column as character
Treat 99 as a valid numeric value and include it in means
T13.explanation: Sentinel codes must be declared with na.strings or recoded, otherwise they silently contaminate every summary statistic.

T13.stem: When reading a fixed-width file, the essential extra information required is:
options: The number of rows
The file encoding only
The sampling design
The column widths or positions
T13.explanation: Fixed-width files carry no delimiters, so the layout of start and end positions must be supplied from the record specification.

T14.stem: To produce mean expenditure by district from a household data frame, the appropriate operation is:
options: Group by district, then summarise the mean
Reshape to wide format, then average the columns
Sort by district, then take the overall mean
Filter to one district at a time and bind the rows
T14.explanation: Group-then-summarise is the standard split-apply-combine idiom and returns one row per district.

T14.stem: Data in 'long' format store one observation per:
options: Survey round
District, aggregated
Unit-and-variable combination, in a single value column
Household, with variables across columns
T14.explanation: Long format stacks measurements with a key column naming the variable; wide format spreads them across separate columns.

T14.stem: A left join of households to a district lookup table produces more rows than the household table had. The most likely cause is:
options: The lookup table being sorted differently
Duplicate district keys in the lookup table
A missing value in the household table
Using left instead of inner join
T14.explanation: A left join preserves every left row and multiplies against duplicate matches on the right. Deduplicate the lookup before joining.

T14.stem: Computing a mean in R when the vector contains NA returns NA unless you:
options: Convert the vector to a factor
Sort the vector
Pass na.rm = TRUE, having first decided that dropping them is appropriate
Increase the working precision
T14.explanation: na.rm silences the NA but is a substantive decision: dropping missing values assumes they are missing at random.

T15.stem: A weighted mean should be used instead of an unweighted mean whenever:
options: Units were selected with unequal probabilities
The variable is skewed
The sample is larger than 1000
Some values are missing
T15.explanation: Unequal selection probabilities mean the sample does not mirror the population. Weights restore representativeness.

T15.stem: Applying design weights to point estimates but computing standard errors as if the sample were simple random will:
options: Be correct in both respects
Produce an error in most software
Give correct estimates with understated standard errors
Give incorrect estimates with correct standard errors
T15.explanation: This is the most common analysis mistake with complex survey data: the estimate is fine, the stated precision is optimistic.

T15.stem: The main reason to write analysis as a script rather than clicking through a GUI is that a script:
options: Requires less memory
Runs faster
Can be re-run to reproduce the exact published figures
Removes the need for documentation
T15.explanation: Reproducibility is the point: when a figure is queried months later, the script regenerates it exactly.

T15.stem: Setting a random seed before an imputation or a bootstrap ensures that:
options: The same results are obtained on every re-run
The sample becomes representative
Variance estimates are correct
The results are unbiased
T15.explanation: A seed fixes the pseudo-random stream. It buys reproducibility only; it makes nothing statistically more valid.

T16.stem: The National Industrial Classification classifies a unit according to its:
options: Employment size band
Occupation of its workers
Legal ownership form
Economic activity
T16.explanation: NIC classifies what the unit produces. NCO classifies what individual workers do.

T16.stem: The correct hierarchy of the NIC, from broadest to narrowest, is:
options: Group, class, section, division
Class, group, division, section
Section, division, group, class
Division, section, class, group
T16.explanation: Sections carry alphabetic codes; divisions, groups and classes progressively add digits to the numeric code.

T16.stem: An establishment both mills flour and runs a small retail counter. Under NIC it should be classified by:
options: The retail activity, since it faces the customer
Whichever activity employs more workers
The activity listed first in its registration
The activity accounting for the greatest value added
T16.explanation: The principal activity rule uses the largest share of value added, with employment or turnover as practical proxies.

T16.stem: A unit that assembles garments entirely from material owned by another firm, for a fee, is classified under:
options: Business services
Transport and storage
Wholesale trade
Manufacturing, because the transformation activity determines the class
T16.explanation: Physical transformation places the unit in manufacturing regardless of who owns the inputs; this contract-work case is a classic coding trap.

T17.stem: The National Classification of Occupations classifies:
options: The industry of the employing unit
The kind of work a person performs
The wage band of the worker
The educational qualification held
T17.explanation: NCO describes the job itself. Two people in the same industry can hold very different occupations.

T17.stem: In the NCO, the concept of 'skill level' broadly corresponds to:
options: The salary the job commands
The number of years the person has worked
The size of the employing establishment
The complexity and range of tasks in the job
T17.explanation: Skill level reflects task complexity, usually associated with a level of education or training, not tenure or pay.

T17.stem: An accountant employed by a textile mill is coded in NIC and NCO respectively as:
options: Accounting services, and textile occupation
Textile manufacturing in both
Textile manufacturing, and accounting occupation
Accounting services in both
T17.explanation: NIC follows the employer's activity, NCO follows the worker's job. Conflating the two is the most frequent classification error.

T17.stem: 'Skill specialisation' in the NCO refers to the:
options: Field of knowledge, tools and materials the job involves
Sector of the economy
Length of the training programme
Seniority of the post
T17.explanation: Skill level sets the broad major group; skill specialisation distinguishes occupations within that level.

T18.stem: A field return records activity as 'shop'. The correct action by the coder is to:
options: Code it as manufacturing by default
Leave the field blank
Assign the most common retail code
Refer it back for more detail, since the description is too vague to code
T18.explanation: Guessing propagates an error into the published aggregate. Insufficient descriptions should be queried, not resolved by assumption.

T18.stem: The most common cause of misclassification between NIC and NCO in field returns is:
options: Coding at too detailed a level
Use of the previous year's classification version
Illegible handwriting
Recording the employer's industry in the occupation field
T18.explanation: Enumerators frequently write 'railways' or 'hospital' as the occupation. The occupation field needs the job, not the workplace.

T18.stem: Independent double-coding of a subsample of returns is used to:
options: Replace the need for a coding manual
Reduce the sample size needed
Speed up the coding operation
Measure the coding error rate
T18.explanation: Two coders working independently on the same descriptions give a direct measure of coding reliability.

T18.stem: When a classification is revised between survey rounds, comparability over time is preserved by:
options: Aggregating to the section level only
Coding everything to the old version indefinitely
Discarding the earlier round
Publishing a concordance between old and new codes
T18.explanation: A concordance maps old codes to new so series can be bridged; back-casting key aggregates usually accompanies it.
